claim: Essay title and author: The Bitter Lesson by Rich Sutton
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "The Bitter Lesson Rich Sutton"

claim: Essay published March 13, 2019
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "March 13, 2019"

claim: The lesson is read from 70 years of AI research
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "The biggest lesson that can be read from 70 years of AI research"

claim: General methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective, by a large margin
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective, and by a large margin"

claim: Underlying reason: Moore's law, the continued exponentially falling cost per unit of computation
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "continued exponentially falling cost per unit of computation"

claim: Most AI research assumed the computation available to the agent was constant, so human knowledge looked like the main way to improve; over a slightly longer time than a typical research project, massively more computation becomes available
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "Most AI research has been conducted as if the computation available to the agent were constant"

claim: Human knowledge helps in the short term; only leveraging computation matters in the long run
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "the only thing that matters in the long run is the leveraging of computation"

claim: Time spent on human knowledge is time not spent on computation; human-knowledge methods complicate things and suit scaling worse
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "Time spent on one is time not spent on the other"

claim: Chess (running-example candidate, first in source): 1997 Kasparov defeat came from massive, deep search
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "the methods that defeated the world champion, Kasparov, in 1997, were based on massive, deep search"

claim: Chess researchers who used human understanding of chess structure were dismayed; said brute force was not general and not how people play
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "it was not a general strategy, and anyway it was not how people played chess"

claim: Go followed the same pattern, delayed by a further 20 years
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "only delayed by a further 20 years"

claim: In Go, human-knowledge efforts to avoid search proved irrelevant or worse once search was applied at scale; learning by self play learned a value function
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "all those efforts proved irrelevant, or worse, once search was applied effectively at scale"

claim: Search and learning are the two most important classes of techniques for using massive computation; both scale arbitrarily
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "Search and learning are the two most important classes of techniques for utilizing massive amounts of computation"

claim: Speech recognition: DARPA-sponsored competition in the 1970s; special methods using knowledge of words, phonemes, vocal tract
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "there was an early competition, sponsored by DARPA, in the 1970s"

claim: Statistical methods based on hidden Markov models (HMMs) did much more computation and won over human-knowledge methods
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "the statistical methods won out over the human-knowledge-based methods"

claim: The win shifted all of natural language processing over decades toward statistics and computation
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "statistics and computation came to dominate the field"

claim: Deep learning uses even less human knowledge and more computation with huge training sets, giving dramatically better speech recognition
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "Deep learning methods rely even less on human knowledge, and use even more computation"

claim: Vision: early methods (edges, generalized cylinders, SIFT features) are discarded; modern deep nets use only convolution and certain invariances and perform much better
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "Modern deep-learning neural networks use only the notions of convolution and certain kinds of invariances"

claim: Bitter lesson observation 1: researchers often build knowledge into their agents
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "AI researchers have often tried to build knowledge into their agents"

claim: Observation 2: it always helps in the short term and is personally satisfying to the researcher
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "this always helps in the short term, and is personally satisfying to the researcher"

claim: Observation 3: in the long run it plateaus and even inhibits further progress
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "in the long run it plateaus and even inhibits further progress"

claim: Observation 4: breakthrough progress arrives by the opposing approach, scaling computation by search and learning
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "breakthrough progress eventually arrives by an opposing approach based on scaling computation by search and learning"

claim: Why bitter: success comes over a favored, human-centric approach
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "it is success over a favored, human-centric approach"

claim: Core statement: building in how we think we think does not work in the long run
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "building in how we think we think does not work in the long run"

claim: Point 1: the great power of general purpose methods that keep scaling with computation; search and learning
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "the great power of general purpose methods, of methods that continue to scale with increased computation"

claim: Point 2: contents of minds are irredeemably complex (space, objects, agents, symmetries); build in only meta-methods that find and capture complexity
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "build in only the meta-methods that can find and capture this arbitrary complexity"

claim: We want agents that can discover like we can, not ones that contain what we have discovered
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "We want AI agents that can discover like we can, not which contain what we have discovered"

claim: Sutton says the field still has not thoroughly learned the lesson
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "we still have not thoroughly learned it"

claim: Timeline of examples: chess 1997, Go about 20 years later, speech 1970s onward, vision (deep learning); illustrative ordering only, Go year not stated
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "delayed by a further 20 years"

claim: Source contains no benchmark numbers or charts; only years, the 70-year span and the 20-year delay are numeric
source: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html + "essay text"
